claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: CDPK4 is a promising drug target to reduce transmission of malaria.
claims.source: Selective inhibitors of CDPK4 were shown to block exflagellation of P. berghei in vivo and of the human parasite P. falciparum in vitro placing CDPK4 as a promising drug target to reduce transmission of malaria (Ojo et al., 2014, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited experimental results.

claims.claim: The molecular functions of CDPK4 remain unknown.
claims.source: Despite the importance of CDPK4 for transmission to the mosquito vector, its molecular functions remain unknown and none of its substrates have been identified.
claims.evidence: This statement describes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claims.claim: None of CDPK4's substrates have been identified prior to this study.
claims.source: Despite the importance of CDPK4 for transmission to the mosquito vector, its molecular functions remain unknown and none of its substrates have been identified.
claims.evidence: This statement describes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claims.claim: CDPK4 plays at least three distinct roles during male gametogenesis.
claims.source: By combining reverse and chemical genetics with molecular and cellular phenotyping, we found that CDPK4 plays at least three distinct roles during male gametogenesis and we identified three effectors mediating each of these roles.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Three effectors mediating each of CDPK4's roles have been identified.
claims.source: By combining reverse and chemical genetics with molecular and cellular phenotyping, we found that CDPK4 plays at least three distinct roles during male gametogenesis and we identified three effectors mediating each of these roles.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Compound 1294 was found to inhibit P. falciparum exflagellation through CDPK4.
claims.source: One of these, compound 1294, was found to inhibit P. falciparum exflagellation through CDPK4 (Ojo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: CDPK4S147M-3xHA parasites show a fitness cost preventing exflagellation.
claims.source: We however discovered that introduction of both a C-terminal 3xHA epitope tag and a S147M substitution imposed a fitness cost on CDPK4 function preventing exflagellation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Exflagellation is delayed in CDPK4-3xHA parasites.
claims.source: Investigation of the effect of each single modification revealed exflagellation is delayed in CDPK4-3xHA but not in CDPK4S147M parasites.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Exflagellation is not delayed in CDPK4S147M parasites.
claims.source: Investigation of the effect of each single modification revealed exflagellation is delayed in CDPK4-3xHA but not in CDPK4S147M parasites.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: S147M substitution only imposes a minor cost that does not impact on exflagellation on its own.
claims.source: This indicates that a S147M substitution only imposes a minor cost that, on its own, does not impact on exflagellation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claims.claim: CDPK4S147M transgenic parasites showed a ~ 50 fold decrease in exflagellation susceptibility to 1294 compared to the parental wild-type strain.
claims.source: Compared to the parental wild-type strain, CDPK4S147M transgenic parasites showed a ~ 50 fold decrease in exflagellation susceptibility to 1294.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 1 µM 1294 blocked exflagellation by specifically targeting CDPK4.
claims.source: Importantly, 1 µM 1294 blocked exflagellation by specifically targeting CDPK4 and this concentration was further used this study (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating specificity through the resistant mutant.

claims.claim: CDPK4 activity is required between 10 and 20 s to initiate the first round of DNA replication.
claims.source: CDPK4 activity is required between 10 and 20 s to initiate the first round of DNA replication and the second genome replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: CDPK4 activity is not required for DNA replication per se.
claims.source: CDPK4 activity is however not required for DNA replication per se.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DNA replication proceeds normally when 1294 is added after 20 seconds.

claims.claim: Addition of 1294 prior to activation dramatically reduced the ability of male gametocytes to replicate their genome.
claims.source: Addition of 1294 prior to activation dramatically reduced the ability of male gametocytes to replicate their genome as previously described for CDPK4-KO parasites (Billker et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: 25% of microgametocytes progress to the diploid state when 1294 is added prior to activation.
claims.source: We were however able to detect 25% of microgametocytes progressing to the diploid state but not further to the tetra- or octoploid levels.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: When 1294 was added 20 s after activation, no inhibition of DNA replication was observed.
claims.source: When 1294 was added 20 s after activation, no inhibition of DNA replication was observed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: CDPK4 activity between 0 and 20 s post-activation is important for the 1N/2N and subsequent 2N/4N transitions.
claims.source: Altogether, this reveals that CDPK4 activity between 0 and 20 s post-activation is important for the 1N/2N and subsequent 2N/4N transitions but not for DNA replication per se.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data showing timing of CDPK4 requirement.

claims.claim: Almost no diploid parasites reached the tetraploid state when CDPK4 is inhibited.
claims.source: Interestingly, almost no diploid parasites reached the tetraploid state suggesting that CDPK4 plays a second role between the first and second rounds of genome replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: CDPK4 plays a second role between the first and second rounds of genome replication.
claims.source: Interestingly, almost no diploid parasites reached the tetraploid state suggesting that CDPK4 plays a second role between the first and second rounds of genome replication.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: In DMSO treated parasites, 64% of male gametocytes showed spindle-like structures 1 min after activation.
claims.source: In DMSO treated parasites, 64% of male gametocytes showed spindle-like structures while this proportion decreased to 7% in parasites treated with 1294 (Figure 1D) indicating that CDPK4 activity is also required for mitotic spindle formation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: In 1294 treated parasites, 7% of male gametocytes showed spindle-like structures 1 min after activation.
claims.source: In DMSO treated parasites, 64% of male gametocytes showed spindle-like structures while this proportion decreased to 7% in parasites treated with 1294 (Figure 1D) indicating that CDPK4 activity is also required for mitotic spindle formation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: CDPK4 activity is required for mitotic spindle formation.
claims.source: In DMSO treated parasites, 64% of male gametocytes showed spindle-like structures while this proportion decreased to 7% in parasites treated with 1294 (Figure 1D) indicating that CDPK4 activity is also required for mitotic spindle formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data showing reduced spindle formation when CDPK4 is inhibited.

claims.claim: When 1294 is added 30 s after activation, parasites normally develop to the 8N state and assemble axonemes.
claims.source: To do so, we added 1294 30 s after activation, a time point at which CDPK4 is not required to initiate DNA replication anymore. With such a treatment, parasites normally developed to the 8N state and assembled axonemes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1E.

claims.claim: When 1294 is added 30 s after activation, DNA does not condense, axonemes remain around the nucleus and no exflagellation is observed.
claims.source: However, DNA did not condense, axonemes remained around the nucleus and no exflagellation was observed (Figure 1C and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1E.

claims.claim: A similar phenotype is observed when 1294 is added at 9 min post-activation.
claims.source: A similar phenotype was observed when 1294 was added only seconds prior to the initial exflagellation events at 9 min post-activation (Figure 1C and E–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, 1E, and 1F.

claims.claim: When added at 15 min post-activation, 1294 does not inhibit flagellar beating.
claims.source: However, when added at 15 min post-activation, 1294 did not inhibit flagellar beating (Figure 1G) or ookinete formation and motility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 parts 9 and 10).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: When added at 15 min post-activation, 1294 does not inhibit ookinete formation and motility.
claims.source: However, when added at 15 min post-activation, 1294 did not inhibit flagellar beating (Figure 1G) or ookinete formation and motility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 parts 9 and 10).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 parts 9 and 10.

claims.claim: CDPK4 activity is redundant between 30 s and 9 min after activation.
claims.source: Altogether, this shows that CDPK4 activity seems to be redundant between 30 s and 9 min after activation but is further required at a late stage immediately preceding the onset of axoneme motility, DNA condensation and cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data showing no effect of 1294 addition during this time window.

claims.claim: CDPK4 is required at a late stage immediately preceding the onset of axoneme motility, DNA condensation and cytokinesis.
claims.source: Altogether, this shows that CDPK4 activity seems to be redundant between 30 s and 9 min after activation but is further required at a late stage immediately preceding the onset of axoneme motility, DNA condensation and cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data showing effects of 1294 addition at 9 min.

claims.claim: A total of 150 proteins were immunoprecipitated in both CDPK4-3xHA and CDPK4-2xmyc lysates after cross-linking but not in a WT control.
claims.source: A total of 150 proteins were immunoprecipitated in both CDPK4-3xHA and CDPK4-2xmyc lysates after cross-linking but not in a WT control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 parts 1 to 3 and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: MCM2-7/Cdt1 and ORC proteins are the most enriched molecular components in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates.
claims.source: MCM2-7/Cdt1 and ORC proteins that are part of the pre-replicative complex represented the most enriched molecular components (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Proteins of the microtubule cytoskeleton were enriched in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates.
claims.source: Proteins of the microtubule cytoskeleton and of the replisome were also enriched including polymerases α, δ, and ε, the proliferating nuclear antigen, replication factor C complexes and replication factor A.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: Proteins of the replisome were enriched in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates, including polymerases α, δ, and ε, the proliferating nuclear antigen, replication factor C complexes and replication factor A.
claims.source: Proteins of the microtubule cytoskeleton and of the replisome were also enriched including polymerases α, δ, and ε, the proliferating nuclear antigen, replication factor C complexes and replication factor A.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: 178 proteins are immunoprecipitated with both CDPK4-3xHA and MCM5-3xHA including all components of the ORC and the MCM complex.
claims.source: We found 103 proteins interacting with CDPK4-3xHA, CDPK4-2xmyc and MCM5-3xHA indicating that CDPK4 and MCM5 share an overlapping molecular environment (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: CDPK4 represented one of the most abundant interactors of MCM5-3xHA.
claims.source: Consistently, CDPK4 represented one of the most abundant interactors of MCM5-3xHA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: CDPK4 is part of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex.
claims.source: Altogether this suggests that CDPK4 is part of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex and may regulate the pre-replicative complex to initiate DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: CDPK4 may regulate the pre-replicative complex to initiate DNA replication.
claims.source: Altogether this suggests that CDPK4 is part of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex and may regulate the pre-replicative complex to initiate DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the interaction data and known functions.

claims.claim: Cytoskeletal proteins predicted to be components of the microgamete axonemes were the most abundant and significantly enriched cellular components in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates 10 min after activation.
claims.source: Cytoskeletal proteins predicted to be components of the microgamete axonemes (Talman et al., 2014) were the most abundant and significantly enriched cellular components (p-value=5.10−4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Most cytoskeletal components were also enriched in non-activated gametocytes.
claims.source: It is however important to note that most of this cellular component was also enriched in non-activated gametocytes and that cytoskeletal proteins are abundant in male gametocytes (Khan et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Nuclear proteins involved in DNA replication were much less abundant in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates at 10 min compared to earlier time points.
claims.source: Nuclear proteins involved in DNA replication were nevertheless much less abundant compared to earlier time points (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: Traces of CDPK4 were found to be incorporated in exflagellated male gametes.
claims.source: Traces of CDPK4 were also found to be incorporated in exflagellated male gametes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 parts 4 and 5 - [Talman et al., 2014]) in accordance with a role in the initiation of axoneme activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Six proteins showed up to 8-fold increase in abundance in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates upon gametocyte activation which was not observed when CDPK4 was inhibited.
claims.source: For 215 out of the 221 proteins immunoprecipitated with CDPK4-3xHA under all conditions, no obvious differences were detected between the three conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 part 8). However six proteins showed up to 8-fold increase in abundance upon gametocytes activation which was not observed when CDPK4 was inhibited (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Among the six proteins showing increased abundance upon activation were ORC1, ORC2, and ORC5.
claims.source: Among these proteins were ORC1, ORC2, and ORC5, while the three remaining proteins were not functionally annotated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: PBANKA_110290 likely corresponds to a homologue of Cdc6.
claims.source: PBANKA_110290 contained an AAA ATPase domain and a HMM profile analysis indicated that its closest homologue in human and yeast was Cdc6.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and homology searches.

claims.claim: PBANKA_134880 likely corresponds to a homologue of ORC4.
claims.source: Similarly, the closest homologue of PBANKA_134880 was ORC4 in human and yeast.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and homology searches.

claims.claim: PBANKA_051390 likely corresponds to a homologue of ORC3.
claims.source: Finally, homologues of PBANKA_051390 were only found in Plasmodium and Babesia but encoded a PF07034 PFAM domain corresponding to the N-terminus of ORC3.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and domain identification.

claims.claim: 30% of MCM5-3xHA was present in the high salt fraction in non-activated gametocytes.
claims.source: Western blot analysis showed that 30% of MCM5-3xHA was present in the high salt fraction in non-activated gametocytes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The ratio of MCM5-3xHA in the high salt fraction almost doubled 15 s after activation.
claims.source: This ratio almost doubled 15 s after activation but remained unchanged in the presence of 1294 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The ratio of MCM5-3xHA in the high salt fraction remained unchanged in the presence of 1294.
claims.source: This ratio almost doubled 15 s after activation but remained unchanged in the presence of 1294 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Loading of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex onto ORC1-5/Cdc6 complex happens around 15 s after activation of gametogenesis and requires active CDPK4.
claims.source: Altogether, this suggests that loading of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex onto ORC1-5/Cdc6 complex happens around 15 s after activation of gametogenesis and requires active CDPK4.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the co-immunoprecipitation and fractionation data.

claims.claim: CDPK4 has been shown to be myristoylated in P. falciparum.
claims.source: CDPK4 has previously been shown to be myristoylated in P. falciparum (Wright et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: CDPK4G2A-2xmyc microgametocytes did not exflagellate.
claims.source: As for CDPK4-KO parasites, CDPK4G2A-2xmyc microgametocytes did not exflagellate while a CDPK4-2xmyc control was not impaired (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: More than 85% of CDPK4G2A-2xmyc gametocytes remained haploid.
claims.source: Consistently, more than 85% of CDPK4G2A-2xmyc and CDPK4-KO gametocytes remained haploid while 28% of CDPK4-2xmyc gametocytes became octoploid.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: 65% of CDPK4G2A-2xmyc gametocytes showed spindle-like structures.
claims.source: However 65% showed spindle-like structures showing that CDPK4 myristoylation is important to initiate the first round of DNA replication but nor for mitotic spindle assembly (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CDPK4 myristoylation is important to initiate the first round of DNA replication but not for mitotic spindle assembly.
claims.source: However 65% showed spindle-like structures showing that CDPK4 myristoylation is important to initiate the first round of DNA replication but nor for mitotic spindle assembly (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data comparing G2A mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: CDPK4-2xmyc shows two bands on Western blots: one around 63 kDa and one around 55 kDa.
claims.source: Western blots of CDPK4-2xmyc revealed a large band in non-activated gametocytes close to the expected size of 63.1 kDa and a second band migrating around 55 kDa (Figure 3B), a pattern that was conserved during gametogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 part 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: In CDPK4G2A-2xmyc extracts, the large isoform migrated slower.
claims.source: In CDPK4G2A-2xmyc extracts, the large isoform migrated slower.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The large CDPK4 isoform is myristoylated.
claims.source: In some instances myristoylation has been shown to accelerate electrophoretic mobility (Demetriadou et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2011) suggesting that the large isoform is myristoylated.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the altered migration pattern of the G2A mutant and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The 55 kDa CDPK4 band did not show a different mobility in the G2A mutant.
claims.source: Conversely, the 55 kDa band did not show a different mobility.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: No significant evidence of CDPK4 palmitoylation was detected using an acyl-RAC assay.
claims.source: Using an acyl-RAC assay, we were however not able to detect significant evidence of CDPK4 palmitoylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 part 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 part 3.

claims.claim: CDPK4 shows a broad cellular distribution in microgametocytes at 0 and 15 s after activation.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence assays on CDPK4-2xmyc and CDPK4-3xHA, revealed that CDPK4 showed a broad cellular distribution in microgametocytes at 0 and 15 s after activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 part 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: No obvious difference in CDPK4G2A-2xmyc localisation was detected at 0 and 15 s after activation.
claims.source: We were however not able to detect any obvious difference in CDPK4G2A-2xmyc localisation at both time points.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 part 4.

claims.claim: Immunoprecipitation of CDPK4-2xmyc and CDPK4G2A-2xmyc did not reveal any significant changes in interacting partners.
claims.source: Similarly, immunoprecipitation of CDPK4-2xmyc and CDPK4G2A-2xmyc did not reveal any significant changes in interacting partners under the tested conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 parts 5 and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: The CDPK4-2xmyc 55 kDa isoform was fully solubilised during hypotonic lysis.
claims.source: The CDPK4-2xmyc 55 kDa isoform was fully solubilised during hypotonic lysis while 90% of the CDPK4-2xmyc large isoform was solubilised during hypotonic lysis and fully released with a subsequent carbonate treatment (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: 90% of the CDPK4-2xmyc large isoform was solubilised during hypotonic lysis and fully released with a subsequent carbonate treatment.
claims.source: The CDPK4-2xmyc 55 kDa isoform was fully solubilised during hypotonic lysis while 90% of the CDPK4-2xmyc large isoform was solubilised during hypotonic lysis and fully released with a subsequent carbonate treatment (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The large isoform in CDPK4G2A-2xmyc lysates was fully solubilised during hypotonic lysis.
claims.source: Interestingly, the large isoform in CDPK4G2A-2xmyc lysates was fully solubilised during hypotonic lysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: A minor population of myristoylated CDPK4-2xmyc was found in the NaCl fraction which was not observed for CDPK4G2A-2xmyc.
claims.source: We found a minor population of myristoylated CDPK4-2xmyc in the NaCl fraction which was not observed for CDPK4G2A-2xmyc.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: A major population of CDPK4 is soluble whereas a minor population of the large CDPK4 isoform is associated with membranes and possibly with chromatin.
claims.source: Altogether this highlights that a major population of CDPK4 is soluble whereas a minor population of the large CDPK4 isoform is associated with membranes and possibly with chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from fractionation data.

claims.claim: The short CDPK4 isoform corresponds to a shorter protein whose translation is initiated at methionine +57.
claims.source: As the short CDPK4 isoform did not appear to be myristoylated, we hypothesised it may correspond to a shorter protein whose translation could be initiated at a second start codon. The only possible second start codon upstream the catalytic domain was methionine +57, which we replaced by a codon coding for an alanine residue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 part 1). The resulting CDPK4M57A-2xmyc line only expressed the large isoform (Figure 3D) confirming that the translation of the 55 kDa isoform is initiated at a second start codon and cannot be myristoylated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that M57A mutation eliminates the short isoform.

claims.claim: Microgametocytes expressing only the large 63 kDa myristoylated isoform progress to the octoploid stage and assemble axonemes but show a dramatic reduction in exflagellation.
claims.source: Phenotyping of this line revealed that microgametocytes only expressing the large 63 kDa myristoylated isoform, progressed to the octoploid stage, assembled axonemes but showed a dramatic reduction in exflagellation compared to a control line (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The large CDPK4 isoform is mainly required to initiate the first round of DNA replication.
claims.source: Altogether this demonstrates that the large CDPK4 isoform is mainly required to initiate the first round of DNA replication while the short non-myristoylated isoform is essential to complete late gametogenesis (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claims.claim: The short non-myristoylated CDPK4 isoform is essential to complete late gametogenesis.
claims.source: Altogether this demonstrates that the large CDPK4 isoform is mainly required to initiate the first round of DNA replication while the short non-myristoylated isoform is essential to complete late gametogenesis (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claims.claim: Either short or long CDPK4 isoforms seem to support mitotic spindle assembly.
claims.source: Interestingly, either short or long CDPK4 isoforms seem to support mitotic spindle assembly.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from experimental data showing spindle formation in both G2A and M57A mutants.

claims.claim: Nineteen peptides were found to be thiophosphorylated by AS-CDPK4S147G.

claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: SOC1, SOC2 and SOC4 are phosphorylated by AS-CDPK4S147G and could represent early effectors of CDPK4.
claims.source: Among these latter, SOC1, SOC2 and SOC4 are phosphorylated by AS-CDPK4S147G and could represent early effectors of CDPK4.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from combining AS-kinase and phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: GAP40 and SOC3 were not differentially phosphorylated in the CDPK4-KO line but were robustly identified as phosphorylated by AS-CDPK4S147G and could represent CDPK4 effectors to control late gametogenesis.
claims.source: Conversely, GAP40 and SOC3 were not differentially phosphorylated in the CDPK4-KO line but were robustly identified as phosphorylated by AS-CDPK4S147G and could represent CDPK4 effector to control late gametogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from combining AS-kinase and phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: GAP40 could not be deleted in asexual stages, suggesting an essential role in erythrocytic asexual multiplication.
claims.source: GAP40 could not be deleted in asexual stages, suggesting an essential role in erythrocytic asexual multiplication.

results.result: The CDPK4S147M mutation confers ~50-fold resistance to compound 1294, and 1 µM 1294 specifically targets CDPK4 to block exflagellation.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C45 establish the specificity of compound 1294 for CDPK4 through chemical genetic validation. The resistant mutant demonstrates that 1294 acts on-target, providing a critical tool for temporal dissection of CDPK4 function. The data in Figure 1A directly support both claims.

results.result: CDPK4 activity is required between 10-20 seconds post-activation to initiate the first round of DNA replication, but is not required for DNA replication per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 collectively demonstrate through time-course inhibitor addition experiments that CDPK4 acts during a narrow temporal window to trigger S-phase entry. The observation that 25% of cells reach 2N when inhibitor is added early (C49) but 0% progress further, combined with normal replication when inhibitor is added at 20s (C50), strongly supports a role in initiation rather than replication itself. Figure 1B provides clear experimental support.

results.result: CDPK4 activity is required for mitotic spindle formation, with inhibition reducing spindle-positive cells from 64% to 7%.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 establish a second role for CDPK4 in mitotic spindle assembly. The dramatic reduction in spindle formation upon CDPK4 inhibition (C54-C55) and the observation that diploid parasites fail to progress to tetraploid (C52) suggest CDPK4 is required between successive rounds of replication. Immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C-D provide direct visual and quantitative evidence.

results.result: CDPK4 activity is required at a late stage (immediately before exflagellation at ~9 min) to initiate axoneme motility, DNA condensation, and cytokinesis, but is dispensable between 30s and 9 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 define a third temporal window of CDPK4 requirement. When 1294 is added at 30s or 9 min, parasites complete DNA replication and axoneme assembly but fail to exflagellate (C57-C59), while addition at 15 min has no effect (C60-C61). This demonstrates CDPK4 acts to trigger motility rather than being required for axoneme structure. The phenotypic data in Figure 1C, E-G are compelling.

results.result: CDPK4 is part of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex in non-activated gametocytes, with MCM and ORC proteins being the most enriched components in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 establish through co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry that CDPK4 physically associates with the pre-replicative complex. The reciprocal immunoprecipitation with MCM5-3xHA (C68-C69) and GO term enrichment (C65) provide strong evidence. However, C70 is an inference rather than direct demonstration that CDPK4 is a stable complex member versus a transient interactor. The mass spec data in Figure 2A-B and Supplementary file 1 support these claims.

results.result: Upon activation, six proteins including ORC1, ORC2, ORC5, and putative homologues of Cdc6, ORC4, and ORC3 show increased association with CDPK4, and MCM5-3xHA chromatin enrichment doubles at 15s in a CDPK4-dependent manner, suggesting CDPK4 facilitates loading of the MCM2-7/Cdt1 complex onto the ORC1-5/Cdc6 complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 provide mechanistic insight into how CDPK4 regulates S-phase entry. The dynamic changes in protein interactions (C76-C77) and chromatin fractionation (C81-C83) occurring at 15s post-activation align with the temporal requirement established earlier. The identification of ORC homologues (C78-C80) through sequence analysis is reasonable though not experimentally validated. Figure 2C-D provide key supporting data, though the fractionation experiment (C81-C83) would benefit from additional replicates given the quantitative nature of the claim.

results.result: The CDPK4G2A mutation, which prevents myristoylation, blocks exflagellation and DNA replication (>85% remain haploid) but does not prevent mitotic spindle formation (65% show spindles), indicating myristoylation is required for initiating DNA replication but not for spindle assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 demonstrate through genetic analysis that myristoylation differentially regulates CDPK4 functions. The G2A mutant phenocopies CDPK4-KO for DNA replication but retains spindle assembly capability, providing clear functional separation. Figure 3A provides quantitative support for all claims. The inference in C89 is well-supported by the data.

results.result: CDPK4 exists as two isoforms (63 kDa and 55 kDa), with the large isoform being myristoylated as evidenced by altered migration of the G2A mutant, while the small isoform is not myristoylated.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 identify two CDPK4 isoforms through Western blot analysis. The differential migration of the large isoform in the G2A mutant (C91) provides evidence for myristoylation (C92), though this inference relies on literature precedent rather than direct myristoylation detection. The unchanged migration of the 55 kDa band (C93) supports it being non-myristoylated. Figure 3B provides clear supporting data, though direct myristoylation detection would strengthen C92.

results.result: Myristoylation does not significantly affect CDPK4 cellular localization or protein-protein interactions under the tested conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 test potential mechanisms by which myristoylation regulates CDPK4. The negative results (no palmitoylation detected, no localization changes, no interaction changes) are important for ruling out these mechanisms. However, the immunofluorescence resolution may be insufficient to detect subtle localization differences (C95-C96), and the interaction studies (C97) may miss transient or weak interactions. Figure 3—figure supplement 1 parts 3-5 support these claims, though the negative results should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: The majority of CDPK4 is soluble, while a minor population of the large myristoylated isoform associates with membranes and possibly chromatin, as shown by differential fractionation behavior between wild-type and G2A mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 use biochemical fractionation to probe myristoylation function. The differential solubility of the large isoform between wild-type and G2A mutant (C99-C100) and detection in NaCl fractions (C101) suggest membrane and/or chromatin association. However, the chromatin association is tentative ("possibly" in C102), and the functional significance of this minor population is unclear. Figure 3C provides supporting data, though the interpretation regarding chromatin requires additional validation.

results.result: The short 55 kDa CDPK4 isoform originates from translation initiation at methionine +57 and is essential for late gametogenesis (exflagellation), while the large myristoylated isoform is mainly required for initiating DNA replication; either isoform can support mitotic spindle assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 elegantly dissect isoform-specific functions through the M57A mutant. The elimination of the short isoform by M57A mutation (C103) and the resulting phenotype (C104) demonstrate that the short isoform is specifically required for late events. The complementary phenotypes of G2A (blocks early) and M57A (blocks late) mutants strongly support the functional division (C105-C106). The observation that either isoform supports spindle assembly (C107) is well-supported. Figure 3D-F provide compelling evidence.

results.result: Nineteen peptides are thiophosphorylated by AS-CDPK4S147G, and 70 phosphopeptides on 61 proteins show CDPK4-dependent phosphorylation at 18s post-activation; SOC1, SOC2, and SOC4 are identified as potential early effectors, while GAP40 and SOC3 are potential late effectors.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 combine analog-sensitive kinase and phosphoproteomics approaches to identify CDPK4 substrates. The convergence of two independent methods (AS-kinase and KO phosphoproteomics) strengthens substrate identification. The temporal classification into early (C110) and late (C111) effectors is logical based on the phosphorylation timing data. Figure 4A-B and Supplementary files 2-3 provide comprehensive supporting data. The use of "could represent" in C110-C111 appropriately indicates these are candidate effectors requiring validation.

results.result: Genetic knockout analysis reveals that SOC1, SOC2, and SOC3 are important for exflagellation, with SOC1 and SOC2 affecting DNA replication and SOC3 specifically blocking exflagellation without affecting DNA replication or axoneme assembly; SOC4, SOC5, and SOC6 knockouts show no defects, and GAP40 cannot be deleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 validate candidate substrates through reverse genetics. The differential phenotypes of SOC1-3 knockouts versus SOC4-6 controls provide strong evidence for functional relevance. The inability to delete GAP40 (C112) suggests essentiality in asexual stages but limits analysis of its role in gametogenesis. Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 provide supporting data. The phenotypic characterization could be more quantitative for some measurements.

results.result: SOC1 is a CDPK4 effector required for the 1N/2N transition, interacts with MCM proteins and CDPK4, contains SAPS domains conserved in eukaryotes involved in G1/S transitions, and is expressed in asexual stages where its deletion causes fitness costs, suggesting conserved function across life cycle stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C126 characterize SOC1 function and conservation. The phenotype (50% remain haploid, C117) is less severe than CDPK4 inhibition, consistent with additional substrates cooperating (addressed later). The interaction with MCM proteins (C119) and SAPS domain homology (C123) provide mechanistic context. The expression and fitness cost in asexual stages (C124-C125) support broader importance. However, the diffuse cytoplasmic localization (C120) is puzzling for a protein proposed to regulate nuclear DNA replication. Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 support these claims.

results.result: SOC2 is a Plasmodium-specific 623 kDa protein with transmembrane and sialidase domains that is processed into multiple isoforms, localizes to mitotic spindles, and is required for completing mitosis to enable subsequent DNA replication rounds; it is also expressed in asexual stages where deletion causes strong fitness costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C144 extensively characterize SOC2. The phenotype (blocks 2N→4N transition, C130) and spindle localization defects (C132) support a role in mitosis. The protein processing (C139-C140) and spindle colocalization (C141) are interesting but the functional significance is unclear. The large size (C134) and domain predictions (C135) are based on sequence analysis. The detection of only a 140 kDa fragment (C136) versus predicted 623 kDa raises questions about protein stability or processing. Figure 5C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 provide supporting data, though the biochemical characterization is incomplete.

results.result: SOC3 is a Plasmodium-specific protein essential for exflagellation but not for DNA replication or axoneme assembly, localizes to axonemes, is specifically expressed in male gametocytes, and represents a crucial effector for completing cytokinesis by activating axoneme motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C152 characterize SOC3 as a late-stage effector. The complete block of exflagellation without affecting earlier processes (C145-C146) and axonemal localization (C148) strongly support a role in motility activation. The Plasmodium-specific phylogenetic distribution (C151) and male gametocyte-specific expression (C149) are consistent with a specialized function. The inference that SOC3 is "crucial" (C147) and controls "activation of axoneme motility" (C152) is well-supported by the phenotype. Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 provide strong supporting evidence.

results.result: Deletion of SOC1 and SOC2 does not block cell cycle transitions as completely as CDPK4 inhibition, suggesting additional CDPK4 substrates cooperate with SOC1 and SOC2.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C154 acknowledge the incomplete phenotypes of individual substrate knockouts compared to kinase inhibition. This is an important observation suggesting functional redundancy or additional substrates. The inference in C154 is logical and appropriately cautious. This result contextualizes the substrate identification as incomplete rather than comprehensive.

results.result: Multiple kinases and phosphatases control male gametogenesis, and phosphoproteomics reveals a broad phosphorylation-dependent response between 0-18s, suggesting a complex regulatory network underlies DNA replication initiation and mitotic spindle assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C157 place CDPK4 in broader context. The citations to other kinases/phosphatases (C155) and the phosphoproteomics data (C156) support complexity. However, C157 is largely speculation ("likely") about network properties that are not directly tested. The claim is reasonable but represents interpretation rather than demonstrated result. The phosphoproteomics data in Supplementary file 3 support C156.

results.result: Complete deletion of SOC3 blocks exflagellation entirely, suggesting it may be a focal component for axoneme motility activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C159 highlight the non-redundant nature of SOC3 function. The complete block (C158) contrasts with partial phenotypes of SOC1/SOC2 knockouts, supporting the inference that SOC3 is "focal" (C159). However, "focal" is somewhat vague—it could mean non-redundant, rate-limiting, or structurally central. The data support non-redundancy but don't distinguish between these possibilities. Figure 5E provides supporting data.

results.result: CDPK4 activity is essential during two short temporal windows (10-30s and immediately before exflagellation), is activated by PKG-dependent Ca2+ mobilization, and requires myristoylation for early but not late functions, suggesting CDPK4 integrates multiple regulatory signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C165 synthesize the temporal and regulatory findings. The two activity windows (C160) are well-established by the inhibitor studies. The Ca2+ activation (C162) is from prior work. The myristoylation requirement for early functions (C163) is demonstrated by the G2A mutant. The observation that both isoforms support spindle assembly (C164) and that myristoylation is dispensable in the M57A context (C165) are well-supported. The inference about signal integration (C161) is reasonable. This result effectively summarizes key regulatory features.

results.result: Full-length non-myristoylated CDPK4 is active in vitro, and the N-terminal 56 amino acids may represent a regulatory domain controlling nuclear functions, based on the observation that many myristoylated proteins localize to the nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C169 speculate about the function of the N-terminal extension. The in vitro activity of non-myristoylated CDPK4 (C166) is from prior work and supports C167. However, C168 cites human data about myristoylated proteins, and C169 extrapolates this to CDPK4 without direct evidence. The speculation is reasonable but unsupported by data in this study. The fractionation data (C101-C102) provide weak support for nuclear association, but this is a minor population and not definitively chromatin-associated.

results.result: CDPK4 is a promising transmission-blocking drug target, with bumped kinase inhibitors like 1294 blocking transmission in vivo and showing broad-spectrum anti-protozoal activity; CDPK4's multiple essential functions likely explain its strict essentiality for transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C173 discuss translational implications. The drug target potential (C170) and in vivo efficacy (C171) are from prior work. The inference that multiple functions explain essentiality (C172) is logical and supported by this study's findings. The broad-spectrum activity (C173) is from other work. These claims appropriately contextualize the findings but don't represent new results from this study.

results.result: CDPK4 has been reported to be important for sporozoite motility and oocyst formation in Plasmodium, and its functional orthologue TgCDPK1 is essential for egress and invasion in Toxoplasma gondii, suggesting CDPK4 is a pleiotropic regulator across multiple life cycle stages and biological processes in Apicomplexa.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C177 place CDPK4 in broader biological context through literature. The prior reports (C174-C176) are appropriately cited. The speculation about pleiotropic regulation (C177) is reasonable given the multiple roles identified here and in other systems, though "broad spectrum regulator" is somewhat vague. These claims provide useful context but represent synthesis of literature rather than new findings.

results.result: DNA replication kinetics during male gametogenesis show that ~85% of gametocytes are haploid at 0 min, diploid parasites peak at 30s-1 min, tetraploid at 2-5 min, and 75% reach octoploid by 6 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C181 establish the baseline kinetics of DNA replication that provide context for interpreting CDPK4 inhibition experiments. The FACS data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 part 8 directly support these claims. This is important methodological groundwork but represents characterization rather than a major finding about CDPK4 function.

results.result: At 10 min post-activation, cytoskeletal proteins are the most abundant components in CDPK4 immunoprecipitates, though most are also present in non-activated gametocytes; nuclear replication proteins are much less abundant than at earlier timepoints, and traces of CDPK4 are incorporated into exflagellated gametes.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 describe the late-stage CDPK4 interactome. The enrichment of cytoskeletal proteins (C72) is statistically significant but the authors appropriately note these are abundant proteins also present at earlier stages (C73), raising questions about specificity. The decreased nuclear protein abundance (C74) is consistent with CDPK4's changing roles over time. The detection in gametes (C75) supports a late function. However, the functional significance of cytoskeletal protein interactions remains unclear. Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provide supporting data.

results.result: CDPK4 controls three essential processes during male gametogenesis: (1) a myristoylated isoform initiates genome replication within 20 seconds via a SAPS-domain protein (SOC1), (2) CDPK4 is required for mitotic spindle assembly via phosphorylation of a microtubule-associated protein (SOC2), and (3) a non-myristoylated isoform activates flagellar motility to complete cytokinesis via an uncharacterized flagellar protein (SOC3).
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C8 and C37-C38 represent the core findings synthesized in the abstract and introduction. All three roles are well-supported by the temporal inhibitor studies, genetic analysis of isoforms, substrate identification, and knockout phenotypes described in the grouped results above. The identification of three effectors (SOC1-3) mediating these roles is a major achievement. The integration of chemical genetics, proteomics, and reverse genetics provides strong multi-faceted support. This represents the primary contribution of the manuscript.
